desc:
Consider the Fibonacci numbers 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, ... (each is the sum of the two before it; the value 1 is listed once). Count the ways to write n as a sum of distinct numbers from this list, where two ways are different if the sets of numbers used are different (order is irrelevant).

Examples: n = 8 has 3 ways (8, 5+3, 5+2+1); n = 4 has 1 way (3+1); n = 6 has 2 ways (5+1, 3+2+1).
hints: Only about 45 Fibonacci numbers are at most 2·10<sup>9</sup>. A subset DP over sums is impossible for such n, but a search over the 45 numbers might still be small.
Process Fibonacci numbers from the largest to the smallest, deciding take / skip while tracking the remaining target.

Prune with a bound: the sum of the Fibonacci numbers 1..F_i equals F_{i+2} - 2 (for this list), so if the remaining target exceeds the sum of all unused smaller numbers the branch is dead. With this bound and memoisation on (index, remaining) only about two remainders stay alive per level.
editorial: Let the list be F_1 = 1, F_2 = 2, F_3 = 3, F_4 = 5, ... and pre[i] the sum of the first i of them. Define count(i, r) as the number of ways to form r using a subset of F_1..F_i. Then count(i, r) = count(i-1, r) + count(i-1, r - F_i) (the second term only if r ≥ F_i), count(0, 0) = 1, and count(i, r) = 0 whenever r > pre[i].

The bound looks innocent but is what makes this fast. Because each Fibonacci number is less than the sum of all smaller ones plus 2, the only remainders that can still be completed at level i lie in a window of length about F_{i+2} below pre[i], while taking or skipping F_i changes r by exactly F_i. In practice at most two distinct remainders survive per level, so the memo holds O(log n) states (roughly 90 here). Time O(log n) with memoisation, space O(log n). This also explains why the answer grows only slowly with n.
